operation_proposals.why_no_existing_operation: The catalog has partition and selection primitives that can represent documented window extraction or retention, but it has no dedicated operation whose interface distinguishes truncating an overlength sequence to a fixed window from general partitioning.

The paper documents calculation of a mean GERP score for each window. Existing normalization, ranking, and selection operations do not represent the score aggregation itself, so the calculation remains an opaque boundary.
The paper explicitly averages sub-token embeddings for each vocabulary item or sequence. Existing operations do not expose mean aggregation over a sub-token axis.

The catalog contains sampling, ranking, and selection, but no operation representing beam-maintained partial hypotheses and beam-score search. The sequence-generation search therefore remains an opaque boundary.
The catalog has no dimensionality-reduction operation representing t-SNE visualization, so the documented t-SNE stage remains an opaque boundary.

evidence.quote: We curate sequence data along with corresponding textual annotations from the Nucleotide (nt) Database of the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) up to April, 2023. These data encompass genomic DNA and RNA sequences derived across diverse species. Employing a sliding window approach, we truncate sequences longer than 3000 bp to 3000 bp. Sequences with length less than 200 bp are excluded. We filter out sequences containing equal to or more than two consecutive N nucleotides.

We design the prompts to organize the sequence data with the text annotations as feature-ordered input for model pre-training ( Supplementary Table 1 ). The prompt is composed of three modules: 1. an instruction; 2. a nucleotide sequence; 3. an annotation.

The data were tokenized with the byte pair encoding (BPE) algorithm 11 . We train the tokenizer using nucleotide sequences and texts of wiki-103 dataset 12 . SentencePiece 13 is employed as the subword tokenizer, resulting in a dictionary containing 32, 001 tokens. Subsequently, the nucleotide sequences and text annotations are partitioned into sentence-based chunks. We include a special token <s> at the beginning and a special token </s> at the end of the sequence. Each chunk is further tokenized using the trained tokenizer. The max length of input sequence is set to 601 tokens.

We designed prompts to structure the sequences and their corresponding natural language descriptions as model input ( Figure 1A ; Supplementary Table 1 ). The input underwent chunking into subword tokens, followed by embedding through the token embedding layer.
